strengths: The main idea of the paper is to speed-up the RGB-based mapping process by using key ideas published recently – (1) A factorized radiance field representation that was proposed in by Chen et al 2022 to make radiance field learning more efficient, and (2) leveraging the concept of learning a depth covariance function and using it for monocular depth estimation. The individual ideas are not novel but perhaps they have not been combined earlier in the way it is proposed here.
Using factorised tensor field as scene representation in online neural implicit mapping seems novel. Qualitative comparison also shows its advantage over alternative efficient representation.
The method achieves competitive mapping results compared to previous RGB-D and RGB-based system.

The paper introduces an interesting framework that incorporates depth uncertainty into better pose estimation and mapping. They claim they reach photometric and geometric accuracy comparable to RGB-D cases, but using RGB only.

The motivation behind this work is well-founded. The issues addressed, such as unstable initial pose tracking due to poor initial mapping and the challenge of real-time dense mapping while striving for high-quality maps, are valid concerns.
The exploration of advanced NeRF structures, such as TensorRF, shows promise for more efficient optimization.
Leveraging depth estimation for RGB dense SLAM to expedite convergence is a reasonable approach.
weaknesses: The technical exposition is currently quite poor; the draft needs to be thoroughly revised for better readability, and the poor readability makes it difficult to judge the merits of the main idea proposed in the paper.

The claim that the proposed method is for online mapping, and suitable for real-time mapping, is incorrect; the system has two stages and the whole system including the stage that computes poses is not running in real-time.

It is unclear how the camera poses are computed during the initialization stage or afterwards, and whether they are further refined during the on-the-fly stage; various losses are defined but it is not completely clear how they are used in the algorithm.

The evaluation metric based on L1 depth error using median depth values for relative scale is not appropriate as it does not penalize scale drift; a more appropriate approach is to compute a single relative scale factor for the complete scene reconstruction.

Section 4.1 lacks a clear definition of the factorized neural radiance field G; it is unclear whether G is the same as the NeRF function used in prior work, and the factorization of G is not explained, despite being a core idea in the paper.
The manuscript contains numerous typographical and grammatical errors (e.g., 'scarify', 'we tackle to', 'on-the-fly continue', etc.).
The phrase “where the prior aims to learn mapping without poses” is unclear and needs rephrasing and explanation.
The term “To maintain the function’s stability” is ambiguous; it is unclear what function is referred to and the notion of stability needs proper definition.
It is unclear when the initialization phase ends and the on-the-fly phase starts during the on-the-fly phase description.
In the visibility mask B is used but never defined; its source and computation need clarification.
The phrase “denotes the penetrating light” should be rephrased for clarity.

While the theoretical analysis of problem setup seems interesting, it does not provide new insights beyond existing practice; the decomposition into initialization and on-the-fly optimisation has already been used by previous methods [1].
Some equations in the theoretical analysis are confusing; for example, Eq (2) is called posterior instead of likelihood, and Q and Σ are undefined, leading to dimension mismatches.

The proposed self-supervised SDF supervision in Eq (7) is very similar to the pseudo-SDF supervision used in previous methods [2, 3, 4, 5]; the modification of using rendered depth instead of measured depth is confusing and lacks analysis or ablation study.
In the proposed covariance-guided sampling, the use of σ_n instead of diag(Σ_{l_*}) to measure depth uncertainty is questionable and may be a typo.

Using the uncertainty value to dynamically modulate the truncation distance in the self-supervised SDF loss is problematic because truncation distance should be a scene-specific hyper-parameter and not change per ray; the reason for ray-dependent truncation values is unclear.

The sampling process is very complicated, combining uniform stratified, importance, and covariance depth-guided sampling, but no ablation study is provided to demonstrate its benefit; Eq (9) shows depth variance depends only on sampled pixel location, raising the question of why guided sampling is applied in multiple stages.

The experiments are not thorough; comparisons are limited to two RGB-based methods, missing important baselines such as [1] and [6]; the method uses a strong pre-trained depth prior, making comparison with NICE-SLAM in RGB mode unfair; ablation studies are missing for every proposed component.
The overall structure is not polished; the abstract is too long and vague, and the method sections (2 and 4) are not easy to follow.
Figures miss labels or clear definitions on what is shown.
Many variables in equations are not defined or are defined later in the text.
The results are limited, consisting of only a single page.
Reference citations often require additional parentheses, and some sentences are incomplete, making many procedures hard to understand; the incompleteness of the writing is the main concern.

The evaluation results lack conviction; there is an absence of visualizations for the reconstructed 3D map, 2D novel view synthesis, and pose trajectories, and no 3D metric evaluation of scene reconstruction quality.
The solitary 2D metric in Table 1 raises suspicion; lack of per-scene evaluation results for Orbeez-SLAM and unclear averaging methodology need clarification.
The discrepancy in iMAP's PSNR compared to NICE-SLAM, even inferior to the RGB version of NICE-SLAM, requires an explanation.

The paper should clarify the procedure used to measure speed; it appears that NICE-SLAM is already slow, but the proposed method is even slower, conflicting with the claim of being 'more efficient than other RGB-D methods'; identifying the bottleneck responsible for this discrepancy is essential.
